reviewText: Considering how much music I've listened to and reviewed by these guys, it's surprising to recognize how little I know about them. Although I've listened to (the equivalent of) perhaps a dozen albums worth of music, I still cannot say I understand Guided By Voices, and I like that. They are a band that keeps me guessing, that forces me to listen with my wits as much as my ears, and I like that, too. With lyrics that are as opaque as a kaleidoscope, there just isn't much that is tangible enough to provide a foothold.The most obvious trait of GBV is their tendency to take a song just past the point of creativity, and then record it, unadorned. For music fans who listen creatively, this is great fun, because it forces the listener to hear the song from an angle that is obliquely opposed to most pop music. It isn't ear candy, and without the production values that are now considered `normal' or essential for the pop marketplace, we either hear the song through the gauze of `low-fi' or we ignore it entirely. I hate to admit this, but the average Joe on the street likes his music to be provided for him; let radio rotate a few prefabricated variations on familiar themes, and Joe Public is fine with it. He would hate Guided By Voices, and the reasons are simple. The primary reason is that this band avoids the polish and sheen of production values the way that cats avoid swimming pools. I might not know much about the band themselves, but their work methods seem to be fairly obvious. After a song is written, the recording commences soon afterward. Once the song is set down, it is left in that state as if it were preserved in aspic. It's a strange methodology because it relies on the infinite possibilities of initial creation, but forces the process to end at that point.On Under the Bushes Under the Stars, Guided By Voices allow themselves a bit more leeway with production (just a bit), and the album benefits greatly from it. After all, why can't production (or post-production, for that matter) be used as a creative tool? The five tracks that kick off the album make this point abundantly clear, with an attention to detail that is nowhere near anal, but at least shows some consideration for the intelligent songs they decorate. "Rhine Jive Click", "Burning Flag Birthday Suit" and "The Official Ironman Rally Song" sound exactly like Guided By Voices, but they also sound good enough for commercial airplay. One song, "Don't Stop Now" is a re-recording of an earlier song, and true to what I had said earlier, its arrangement remains absolutely true to the low-fi version it updates, except with a production that suits it better and makes it more appealing. These guys still might not get airplay, but after this album, I can no longer say that it is simply because the band chooses it to be that way. Who knows? If radio stations started playing "Lord of Overstock", maybe Joe Public would hum along.  A  Tom Ryan

reviewText: The Jacksons' 1981 live album is an audio snapshot (too bad there isn't a video release!) of their award-winning "Triumph" world tour.  The opening built so much suspense in anticipating the show's commencement, and the cheers from the crowd leave you guessing what was happening visually.  "Can you feel it" opens the concert and is slightly different than the album version; though it has less punch than the album version, it is taken faster and is more suited for high-energy Jackson shows.  Having the Jackson brothers sing backup for Michael's "Off the Wall" numbers turned out pretty well.  As much as the group was pressing their current offerings ("Triumph," "Destiny," and "Off the Wall"), it is clear that the fans got the biggest thrill from the Motown songs.  The Jacksons performed all four #1 Motown hits, as well as Michael's #1 "Ben."  Although awkard at times with their older voices and Marlon's delivery of Jermaine's former solo lines, the songs are nice.  Other than "Can you feel it," several other songs were performed faster than the album versions.  "This Place Hotel" and "Lovely One" sound great this way.  Also, "Shake Your Body," "Lovely One" and "I'll Be There" feature nice vocal improvs; on the other hand, a few tracks differ very little from the album versions.  As the only live album easily available from the Jackson boys, it is worth a listen, but don't look at is a definitive statement of their musical output.

reviewText: Probably the number one reason that I love Dwight Yoakam is best contained in this album: he's very reminiscent of older, great country artists that played REAL country music such as Buck Owens, Johnny Cash, and Merle Haggard. In a modern country music world of CMT cookie cutter, top 40 pop music wannabes, DY has struck his own unique path.As great as *If There Was a Way* and *Guitars, Cadillacs, Etc., Etc.* are, *This Time* has them all beat. This is simply the best collection of songs by DY on any one album. There's a little bit of everything here and nearly all of it is great songwriting."Pocket of a Clown" was a big country radio smash and is good but is not one of the gems of the album. I agree with another reviewer that "A Thousand Miles from Nowhere" is not only a great song, but was indeed a fitting ending to the excellent film Red Rock West. As the credits roll, the song is a perfect summing up of the main character's situation. "Home for Sale" is another slowed down song about lost love. The title song is a classic honky-tonker very reminiscent of classic Buck Owens. One of my very favorite songs here is "Two Doors Down". Perhaps there's nothing happy about it, but the feeling that comes through seems genuine. "Ain't That Lonely Yet" is another excellent song that probably sums up a lot of broken relationships. "King of Fools" is good stuff as well and "Fast as You" may be the "rockinest" song on the disc. "Lonesome Roads" is a very fitting ending to the album and always reminds me of something Merle Haggard might have played.In short, DY has it all going on. The man is simply a great musician with a great voice and he writes and plays songs that actually mean something. What else could one ask for?

reviewText: The Red Hot Chili Peppers seem to be a bit less "Red Hot" these days. They're still making very good music, but it seems that they have mellowed with age. Just compare Californication to Mother's Milk, The Uplift Mofo Party Plan or even Blood Sugar Sex Magik and you'll see that the RHCPs have definitely chilled out a bit. Pretty much gone is the frantic funk-rap-rock style of earlier days, now the Peppers seem more interested in crafting pretty melodies. This is a much more radio-friendly group than the one that brought us "Give It Away", "Power Of Equality" and "Sir Psycho Sexy".I think Californication is a good album with a lot of great songs, but frankly it just doesn't rock enough. Compared with Blood Sugar Sex Magik which had great songs, a tight groove, plenty of hard-rockers, a lot of funk, and a very high energy level, Californication seems sedated in comparison. Not that that's bad, it's just a new direction for the band. However, I must say that I prefer the old Chili Peppers. There are a few tracks on the album that approach the funky rockin' style of Blood Sugar Sex Magik such as "Around The World", "I Like Dirt" and "Get On Top", but it's mostly polished pop/rock without much of a trace of the Peppers' distinct style.Californication is certainly one of their better albums, but fans of the old-school Chili Peppers may be a bit dismayed. Many of the songs sound tailor-made for radio and are missing that late 80s/early 90s energy. This is a fine album, and I'm glad it was a success, but Blood Sugar Sex Magik went platinum many times over without the benefit of such a radio-friendly sound, and even with the disadvantage of an "explicit lyrics" sticker (meaning no Wal-Mart sales).I enjoy this album, but when I want a taste of the real Red Hot Chili Peppers, I will cue up Mother's Milk or Blood Sugar Sex Magik.

reviewText: The muscle-bound front man for C & C Music Factory may be the one that most associate with the early 90's group, but the real wizards behind the ensemble were Robert Clivilles and the late David Cole.  Taking up where 70's disco and 80's dance left off, the duo billed their music as a melding of rock, soul, funk, pop, and techno.At a little over an hour in length, the album features their number one hits on respective Billboard lists (the title cut, "Here We Go", Things that Make You Go Hmmmm..." and "Just a Touch of Love"). reviewText: Neko as a singer is a total natural with a powerhouse style she has learned to use with more and more subtlety with experience. Her output is still on an upward trajectory in terms of quality which in some ways is quite surpising as she has been at it for a while now and the last album was excellent too. A dedication to songwriting craft and a real love of music required. It is also quite a brave album with a fair few songs varying in style from previous work and i sort of imagine many folks skipping tracks as the style may not be their thing. i think those listeners who like a wide body of music will appreciate this variety. Another reviewer compared her to Kirsty MacColl and i thought that was quite perceptive. Sweet Kirsty. i would recommend forcing this album down through repeat plays without skipping. As an average album buying bloke i like the vocals and tunes and arrangements but i don't massively relate to the lyrical themes of animals, the environment and the natural world which for her may be some sort of worldview or philosophy. Not mine but that's ok. The bit about not skipping i wrote earlier certainly does not apply to the harmless forest music at the end. That i would recommend skipping unless you are an artist painting a tree and need some musical accompaniment. Why not download the mp3 and listen to it while going for a ramble? only kidding. She is quite a vague writer at times leaving the listener to fill in the gaps. Harder not to be vague. don't like the picture on the cover ?? tarantino ?? Love the album itself though and i really hope there's more to come. Beautiful and edgy songs.

reviewText: Truth be told, I didn't become aware of Massive Attack until they released "Teardrop" here in the U.S., and although smitten by that song, I didn't fully explore their music until four years later, when I heard some of their early singles and was inspired to take the plunge into Massive's world. From the sound of this album, that world is one in which you're never alone, just commiserating with the lonely. Semi-stalker anthem "Angel" begins with humming bass, and then builds until it climaxes in distorted menace. On "RisingSon", 3-D and Daddy G juxtapose bizarre lyrics-the former lamenting "cheap beers filled with crocodile tears"; the latter sing-speaking part of the Pete Seeger classic "Where Have All The Flowers Gone"-with a lethal, head-nodding beat."Teardrop" provides the first part of the album's centerpiece, as the Cocteau Twins' Liz Fraser pours her angelic vocal over a staccato beat, punctuated by chilling stabs of piano. Part 2 of the album's centerpiece comes in the form of "Inertia Creeps", wherein music and lyrics combine to create a glorious, claustrophobic track that plays like an open wound. A romping bass line is the compass as 3-D navigates a hellish rap, warning, "inertia keeps/moving up slowly/inertia creeps/moving up slowly". Thankfully, MA insert a break from the murky action via the warm sonic washes of the instrumental "Exchange" (Horace Andy closes the album with an equally compelling vocal version of the song). On the crunching, "Dissolved Girl", we return to the shadows, as Sara Jay purrs her way into oblivion; and an amped up cover of John Holt's "Man Next Door" provides another perfect vehicle for Andy's brawny voice.However, the album really kicks into high gear with the dubby, disturbing trilogy of "Black Milk", the epic title track, and the stunning "Group Four". "Black Milk", which features Fraser on vocals, opens with ghostly piano, and then takes the listener to dub heaven. The sleek title track features 3-D and Daddy G, the latter of whom utters perhaps the most poignant lyric of the entire album when he intones, "you know you had a heart made of stone/you should have let me know". Finally, on "Group Four", 3-D and Fraser share vocal duties over a typical MA beat, then the song careens ever faster until you think it's about to drop off the end of the earth. The aforementioned album-closing vocal version of "Exchange" only slightly melts the ice forest that is "Mezzanine". At the end of the journey through this bruised sonic landscape, the wounds are still fresh, but beginning to heal.

reviewText: The best thing about Smash Mouth is that, as much as they love music, they never take themselves too seriously.  Their sound ranges from sixties party to contemporary pop, with a heavy influence of early rock.  Their lyrics are often satiric or downright humorous, with undercurrents of more serious concerns."Diggin' Your Scene" evokes the late sixties with a beat that one can imagine woman in vinyl mini-skirt dancing to while their stoned guys stand mesmerized by the colored lights.  The lyrics poke fun at the sixties lingo while describing a guy's obsession with a dangerous woman.  The following "I Just Wanna See" has the same kind of fun sound with hippy philosophy:  "Doctors and lawyers race for the ball/And I don't even wanna understand it all/I just wanna see."  "Then The Morning Comes" nods to the Beach Boys and to the surfer movies of the sixties; you can almost see the montage of skinny hippies and girls in polka dot bikini running toward the ocean. Not all the tracks are retro (except for the fact that the album was released in 1999).  The pop chart favorite "All Star" is a catchy tune about embracing the life that fame brings.  Ironically, "Stoned" sounds less retro than one would expect.  The group's foray in reggae ("Road Man") is less successful than the other tracks."Astro Lounge" is rock/pop for those who miss the sixties and seventies -- or wish they had lived through them.  -- Debbie Lee Wesselmann

reviewText: Many years ago, I wouldn't have touched an ABBA CD with a ten foot pole. I was just too darn cool for that! How then does an avid Rock N'Roll fan, who's been collecting classic rock music for close to thirty years suddenly become addicted to the lighter than air, Euro-Pop sounds of the '70s supergroup, ABBA? There are three sources of my ABBA-ization. One reason was that my wife of over ten years, finally got a new car, that actually had a CD player in it. Now, let me tell you, usually my wife has virtually no interest in the subject of music at all! But once she had access to that CD player, the one thing she wanted was ABBA's "Gold: Greatest Hits". At first I was quite resistant! "Ugggh, You want me to listen to that "POP MUSIC??", I protested! But she was persistent and little by little those beautiful voices of Agnetha & Anni-Frid, singing those hook drenched tunes of Benny & Bjorn, slowly began to infiltrate my brain. My ABBA fate was finally sealed. when I saw two different movies. The first is "Muriel's Wedding", an Australian film about an unhappy young women, who escapes her pain listening to our favorite Swedish songbirds. The other film was Spike Lee's "Summer of Sam". Although the film is somewhat gruesome (It's about the famous '70s era serial killings in NYC) it makes a brilliant visualization of my favorite ABBA song, "Dancing Queen". But that did it! I am now truely a huge ABBA fan, collecting both their music and videos. But no matter how much I buy, I always go back to this original "Gold: Greatest Hits" which started it all. The voices are beautiful and the songs have this power to make you unconsiously start tapping your feet. This combination just seems to take me to another place. It dosn't matter if the song's subject matter is happy or sad. It just seems to put a smile on my face. This is especially good if you've had a hard day and just want to lay back and forget about your troubles! My personal favorite tunes include the before mentioned "Dancing Queen, "Mama Mia", the especially addictive "Take a Chance On Me", "Super Trouper" and the beautiful anthem "Thank You for the Music". If you really get down to it, the whole darn album is great! I've gotten to the point, that I'm now driving my wife crazy by playing this CD, whenever we are in the car! Now, just the other day, I suddenly heard my three year old son start singing the words, "see that girl, watch that scene, dig in, Daaaancing Queennnn!!" Uh-Oh, it's caught on to a whole new generation....

reviewText: Pun had skills, no doubt. His 1998 debut "Capital Punishment," was a classic. This album does not measure up to that, but it's still pretty good overall."Watch Those" is a nice track in which  Pun spits those same kinds of wicked lines he mastered on Capital  Punishment. "It's So Hard" finds Pun experimenting with a  different flow, in which he hightens his voice during the middle and end of  each line. It's also rather sad, as he says at the end of the first verse  "I just lost a hundred pounds, I'm tryna live!""New  York Giants" is a hyped up joint, which isn't surprising considering  it features everybody's favorite hyped-up duo, M.O.P. "N*gga  Sh*t" features a dope beat courtesy of Buckwild, but it's far too  short, clocking in at only 1:45. Other standout tracks include "Off  Wit His Head," "Leather Face," and "Laughing At  You."The album trails off slightly at the end, with a few tracks  (and guests) that fail to justify their being on the album.  Overall,  despite it's flaws and short length, "Yeeeah Baby" is still a  worthy buy.R.I.P. Pun

reviewText: Mobb Deep is a very unique rap duo, at least in my collection.  Ghetto stories are nothing very new, but Mobb Deep takes a different approach.  Between the dark production and the reality story-telling, listening to this album puts you in a whole different zone.  Prodigy and Havoc are both pretty good rappers, but it's not fast rapping or wordplay where they excel.  It's the intense, first-person point of view that makes them great. They tell very vivid tales of their battles with rival gangs and robberies and drug sales and police scuffles and the other struggles of gang life.  You can make a perfect picture in your mind.  The production is mostly done by Mobb Deep, with some help from Q-Tip.  It suits the rhymes perfectly.  It's dark and raw straight through.  It has to be carefully done to fit with the stories, and it works.  All through the album you have this picture of a cloudy day in some of the poorest ghettos in Queens in some dark alleyway.  Everything these guys do on this CD fits together like they're painting a picture.  They succeeded.  Highly recommended.

reviewText: Morning View. What a perfect name for this album. I can easily picture myself sitting on the beach on the cover on an early spring morning listenning to this CD. I was first introduced to Incubus with 1997's brilliant S.C.I.E.N.C.E. Incubus' main influences are Faith No More, Primus, Helmet, and The Red Hot Chili Peppers which are all some of my favorite bands. Its obvious that I would take a quick liking to this band from my hometown of Los Angeles. Whether it be Brandon's vocal similarities to the "smooth as silk" Mike Patton, Alex's "fastest gun in the west" funky slap, Jose's amazing work with his Zildjian's, DJ Lyfe's creative scratching, or Mike's "Jazz-to-Funk-to-Metal in 1.2 seconds" riffery, I could not, no matter how hard I tried, get S.C.I.E.N.C.E. out of my CD player. When I first heard "Pardon Me" I thought that Make Yourself may be even better than S.C.I.E.N.C.E. I was beyond disappointed when I heard Make Yourself all the way through. I felt that Incubus had sold out more than any band had sold out before. It took me a long time to see Incubus for what they are. One day I decided to listen to "The Warmth" and for some unknown reason, loved it. I finally realized what Incubus was trying to do, to be a talented band that everyone can like. I am able to accept the fact that Incubus may never produce an experimental masterpiece like S.C.I.E.N.C.E. again as long as they keep up their original and creative ideas.Morning View is mainly a mix of Faith No More styled song structures, Helmet inspired riffery, and Red Hot Chili Pepper inspired melodic-funk numbers. "Nice To Know You" shows Incubus' love for Faith No More with its maniacal speed changes. "Circles" slams the Helmet styled riffery in your face like a sledgehammer. "Circles'" inspiration can even be pinpointed to an exact Helmet track, "Biscuits For Smut". "Just A Phase", "11am", and "Echo" sound like many of the slow funk tracks on the Red Hot Chili Peppers Blood Sugar Sex Magik. Morning View may not be as original as S.C.I.E.N.C.E. or Fungus Amongus, but with influences such as Faith No More, Primus, and Helmet they can't go wrong.

I felt that Incubus had sold out more than any band had sold out before. It took me a long time to see Incubus for what they are. One day I decided to listen to "The Warmth" and for some unknown reason, loved it. I finally realized what Incubus was trying to do, to be a talented band that everyone can like. I am able to accept the fact that Incubus may never produce an experimental masterpiece like S.C.I.E.N.C.E. again as long as they keep up their original and creative ideas.Morning View is mainly a mix of Faith No More styled song structures, Helmet inspired riffery, and Red Hot Chili Pepper inspired melodic-funk numbers. "Nice To Know You" shows Incubus' love for Faith No More with its maniacal speed changes. "Circles" slams the Helmet styled riffery in your face like a sledgehammer. "Circles'" inspiration can even be pinpointed to an exact Helmet track, "Biscuits For Smut". "Just A Phase", "11am", and "Echo" sound like many of the slow funk tracks on the Red Hot Chili Peppers Blood Sugar Sex Magik. Morning View may not be as original as S.C.I.E.N.C.E. or Fungus Amongus, but with influences such as Faith No More, Primus, and Helmet they can't go wrong.

reviewText: Blonde Redhead is one of many bands I found on various 'so you want to get into indie' lists and downloaded essentially at random. Now I must state in advance that I am no afficionado in regards to the styles of music this fairly vague genre encompasses, and that I also have not been very impressed by most of the bands I have heard. However there can be no mistake... Misery is a Butterfly is beautiful music.This album is designed to hit nerves, hard. Every melody is crafted with intent and deliberation, and the progressions are largely orchestral in nature - many moments in this album bring to mind the melodramatic chord pivots of pieces written by Beethoven. Amadeo's voice conjures Thom Yorke post-back alley beating, crying for mercy and a little humanity, please. Kazu's voice provides a ghostly, exhausted alternative to the self-absorbtion of Amedeo. They work in concert beautifully.Almost any song on Misery is a Butterfly could be considered a highlight without much of a stretch. It opens with the deeply sentimental, meloncholic "Elephant Woman," which brings to mind all the saddest moments in a Benji film. The longing rhodes piano and tentative, loping snare drum of "Melody" is a haunting, cynical look through an old shoebox of things you forgot about long ago and maybe didn't want to remember. "Falling Man" is another highlight (but where are the lowlights?), with one of the most bent tearjerk melodies in recent memory. "Doll Is Mine" is the furious protest of someone who is obviously far too disadvantaged to do anything about what is plagueing them. "Maddening Clovd" is clearly the climax of this record, although not necessarily the last good song; It provides a high energy, hopeful beam of light at the end of the tunnel. Even against the brutal melody, the pace of the song seems to suggest "we're still gonna try our best!"A highly recommended album for any fan of indie, alternative rock, or any emotionally impactful form of music. A little sentimental, yes, but that's not inherrantly a bad thing, and this album is evidence of that. Indie seems most likely to be a downhill journey for me from here.

reviewText: One of the greatest artistic triumphs of the past fifty or so years, Blood On The Tracks is a gorgeous musical meditation, a haunting and cathartic exploration of love, loss, and the complexity of human relationships. The songs are emotionally purgative and bottomlessly soulful, full of quiet desolation and breathless longing. The lyrics are sheer poetry, gorgeous free verse hurled across the the entire spectrum of human emotion, glowing with warmth, spite, pain and humor. The music is just as powerful, an intoxicating blend of rock, folk, country, and blues, with lilting melodies colliding over dense atmospheres and wordless apocalyptic imagery. The end result is a masterpiece of emotional expression, a darkly resonant and often harrowing piece of music, a work that is both powerfully complex and instantly accessible, something that speaks to every living breathing human being, everybody who has ever felt love or hate or pain, who's stayed awake late into the night, wondering about the pain in their heart and the losses in their life. At times- like during the utter desolation of "Simple Twist Of Fate" or the spine-tingling story arc of "Tangled Up In Blue," this album commands a power that defies words, that digs its way to the very heart of the human experience, to the loves and hates and horrors that lie at the center of our consciousness. At other times, like in the freewheeling narrative of "Lily, Rosemary, And The Jack Of Hearts" or the wheezing blues of "Meet Me In The Morning," it's simply good fun. But it's always, always brilliant. Indescribably essential.

reviewText: Probably no other bassist played as big a role as Charles Mingus did in helping shape modern jazz, and probably no other recording of Mingus defines his jazz quite the way this does. The first time I listened to this piece, I got completely lost and couldn't make any sense of it. The second time too. By the third time I heard it, everything began falling into place, and I was toe tappin' and neck snappin' in beat with the tunes. Foggy day is probably one of the most interesting "songs" on the CD, simply to listen for how each musician makes their instrument sound like something off of a busy, crowded street when traffic is not going smoothly. With Mingus to pull the tune along, the effects are executed very brilliantly, and will have you smiling at their intricacy and cleverness. This isn't the most approachable CD in the jazz pantheon, but I think it is one everyone will eventually "get", so it is worth adding to your jazz collection. (The title line, by the way, is from The Rebel Set inThe Mystery Science Theater 3000 Collection, Vol. 12 (The Rebel Set / Secret Agent Super Dragon / The Starfighters / Parts: The Clonus Horror), where jazz meets B-movie wise-acres and those who know jazz and love B-movies laugh themselves sick.)

reviewText: This self titled album marks a transitional point in Ross's musical career.She was steeped very deeply in movie acting at this time but still have her songs a sensually soulful bite.And certainly that quality is present on the the vocal pause and release of "Love Hangover",a funky proto disco classic that builds luciously in tempo and was thankfully a HUGE hit for her.This also includes the alluring but meloncaulic theme from'Mahogony' "Do You Know Where Your Going To",this album being the best place to get that song.Her version of "Ain't Nothin' But A Maybe" actually rivals Rufus & Chaka's two year old rendition,despite sounding very similar musically."I Thought It Took A Little Time","After You","Once More In My Lifetime" and a triumphant version of "Smile" deliver slow,sensuas backups in Ross's familiar style,even while tempered by the upbeat soul of "Kiss Me Now".As of this 1976 album Diana Ross hadn't yet lost her original soulful quality to showbiz schmaltz and this album proves that somewhere underneath all that glitter and glam the ol' lead singer of the Supremes is there intact,as she is here!

reviewText: Muse always impresses me. This is some of the most original, creative rock music out there on the scene today. Matt Bellamy is one of the most talented vocalists on the modern rock scene right now. He uses so many timbres and textures with his voice. The music pulls from so many different influences. While there are obvious touches of Radiohead in the music, the songs rock a lot harder than Radiohead ever does. You can hear influences of classical, latin, classic rock and industrial/techno styles. The result is an amazing product with something huge to offer.The music is incredibly dynamic. The opening track, "Take a Bow" builds to an incredible apex of sound. The music is tinged with electronic garneshes of color. The thick arrangements are so well put together and every instrument fits into a beatiful picture. There are many great moments on this album, like the explosive drumming on "Assassin," the latin-esque trumpeting and acoustic guitar in "City of Delusion," the stunning piano work on "Hoodoo," and the breathtaking overdubbed harmonies in the epic closing track "Knights of Cydonia."This album is quite amazing. A wonderful addition to Muse's diverse catalog of exciting music.

reviewText: I recently took out this album for a spin after going several months (maybe a year!) without listening to it.  Nobody makes music quite like this anymore!  This is the album that got me hooked on Sarah.  I happened to get this album and Tori Amos' Under the Pink at the same time.  I wasn't familiar with either one of them at the time, but they were both highly recommended, so I thought I'd give them a try.  I'll admit that this album stayed in its case for quite some time after I bought it, but that's just because I happened to listen to Tori's album first and didn't really listen to anything else for quite some time after that.  But after my Tori fever broke a little, I stuck this one in my player one day and was immediately swept away again, this time by Sarah.I love Sarah's work and she is still putting out great music.  But this will always be my favorite of all her albums.  Maybe its the songs, maybe its the fact that this was the first album of hers that I got into (there's always something about that first album that grabs your heart forever, its like your first love; nothing is quite like it), but Fumbling sounds to me like perfection, and you can't do better than perfection.  Possession was the first song that really grabbed me, not just because its the first song, but because I remembered seeing the video on VH1.  The imagery fit the song so well, and after listening to the rest of the album, I had no trouble putting my own imagery to the rest of the songs.Plenty is one of my favorites, though all the songs are brilliant.  There's nothing quite as meloncholy and heart-wrenching as being betrayed by someone you trusted implicitly.  Circle is a really rocking song and is followed up perfectly with the quiet cool of Ice.  I love the sax solo in Ice, it doesn't really sound like any sax you'd normally hear in pop music.  Hold On is one of my favorite songs ever.  I feel the tears pricking my eyes every time I hear the anguish in her voice over watching the man that she loves suffering and knowing that he will not be with her much longer.  Fear is a sonically different song from just about any song you've probably ever heard and both the music and lyrics are haunting ("From above, they say temptation will destroy our love").  The title track is another one of my favorite songs.  The drums are soft and soothing, especially after the harshness of Fear.  And what better way to start the song after Fear than by singing "All the fear has left me now, I'm not frightened any more".  The chorus is so easy to relate to. Sarah is singing about not denying yourself and your emotions.  "If I shed a tear I won't cage it, I won't fear love".This album helped shape more than just my musical preferences when I was in high school.  It gave me something to relate to, and because of that, I will forever love this collection of songs.  Many of you probably have similar experiences with this album.  For those of you who have never heard it, please don't deny yourself any longer!
summary: I couldn't go on without this disc!

The title track is another one of my favorite songs. The drums are soft and soothing, especially after the harshness of Fear. And what better way to start the song after Fear than by singing "All the fear has left me now, I'm not frightened any more". The chorus is so easy to relate to. Sarah is singing about not denying yourself and your emotions. "If I shed a tear I won't cage it, I won't fear love".This album helped shape more than just my musical preferences when I was in high school. It gave me something to relate to, and because of that, I will forever love this collection of songs. For those of you who have never heard it, please don't deny yourself any longer!

reviewText: Three albums in, and Daft Punk has a greatest hits... well, "anthology", released. Now that's not jumping the gun at all is it? Well, despite the eyebrows that may have been raised in response to this move, what group to better make a self-indulgent cash in other than Daft Punk? After all, they are one of the planet's best house producers ever. All the fan favorites are right here. BAM! Around the World! BAM! Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger! BAM! One More Time! BAM! Technologic! And that's just naming a few. For the life of me, I can't wrap my head around how Rollin' & Scratchin' wound up on here, but I suppose I never will unless I somehow got a chance to ask Daft Punk first-hand. But there's another reason to go all out on this sugary Daft Punk goodness filled compilation.Even if you happen to own all of Daft Punk's first three studio albums, Christo and Bangalter sweeten the deal even more by throwing in four irresistible goodies that are by far enough to make the Daft Punk fan's mouth water. Remember that short little muffled radio music loop that can be heard from "WDPK 83.7 FM" on Homework? That's actually an excerpt. It was a B-Side from the "Da Funk" single, the appropriately titled "Musique", and the delicious masterpiece can be heard in full now since its included as the first track on Musique. The other three tracks included are three Daft Punk remixes, and they are all brilliantly crafted house beauties that should serve as a reminder of why remixing  can be such a good idea in the first place. These four new inclusions by themselves could justify the purchase of Musique for the Daft fan.On the contrary, even if this is your first time diving into the duo's discography, then this is a great starting point. If you thoroughly enjoy this, then its just an appetizer for the fantastic albums and tracks that Daft Punk has put out in the 10+ years before the release of this compilation.P.S. Before you buy, you may want to keep in mind that there appear to be three variations of this anthology. 1) A standard jewel case single disc release which contains simply the hits themselves. 2) A 2-disc digipak with the first standard disc and a second being a DVD which has many of the band's music videos throughout the years, and 3) a 3-disc digipak housed in a beautiful red slipcase, with the first two being the foremetioned discs and the third being the Daft Club remix album in it entirety. Enjoy!(Review revised January 24th, 2014)

reviewText: This is one of Bob Dylan's best works.  It appeared after a couple lame works and a so-so album.  It marked a wonderful "comeback," if you will.  There was an acoustic sensibility that worked.  His harmonica playing worked well.  His voice was, to the extent that it was possible, in good form (sometimes, his vocal rendering of songs becomes somewhat strange)."Tangled up in Blue" is a terrific song, one of the best on this CD and one of the best he ever did.  The images come, one on top of another.  A powerful work."Idiot Wind" hearkens back to an earlier day, when his singing was explicitly political.  This is an angry song, and it works pretty well.  The line when he remarks that the idiot wind interacts with "the Capitol" (sung in a compelling way) highlights this cut."Lily, Rosemary, and the Jack of Hearts" remind me of some of his offbeat, strange, metaphor-riddled works such as "Desolation Row."  Images emerge one after another from this piece."Shelter from the Storm" is a laid back, evocative tune.  It ends up with an upbeat, optimistic feel to it.And on it goes.  No need to mention each song in its turn.  But most of the cuts on this CD are fine pieces of musical art.In short, one of Dylan's best.

reviewText: Let me start off by saying that I didn't really know who Sara Bareilles was prior to this album.  I knew the song "Love Song", but didn't know it was by her.  I saw her name thrown around but I never looked her up.  Then the Grammy Nominations for 2014 were announced and everyone, including myself were surprised to see her name and album in the Album of The Year category.  She beat out critically acclaimed albums by artists such as Justin Timberlake, Kanye West, and Vampire Weekend among others.  So I was interested in hearing what the buzz about this album was about.  I previewed some songs and listened to the lead single "Brave" which has been played in commercials and is really catchy.  I decided to actually purchase the album, even though this type of music isn't usually my preference, especially since I consider myself a manly man.  I still gave her a big chance and bought her album, and here is a track by track review.1. Brave: When I first listened to the song I sensed a familiarity in its sound.  Not my favorite of the album, but very catchy.  Nice motivational feelgood song.  But I'm the type that usually likes the songs not released as the lead single more.  Still a good pop song.  9/102. Chasing the Sun:  This is a great song.  It builds upon itself and the emotions it brings out in the listener is magical.  The last 2 minutes of the song really sound beautiful.  The background vocals toward the end are the perfect sound to accompany strength after a breakup.  Just a great great song and could be a single.  9.5/103. Hercules: My favorite song on the album.  The opening piano riff is unbelievably catchy.  The verses were good at first, but then when I heard the chorus I could feel my soul swooning for her voice.  It is just perfect.  There is also great use of strings in the song toward the end.  Since I'm a guy, I use this song as motivation to be the Hercules for a woman.  Perfect song.  10/104. Manhattan: Not my favorite song, but I'm sure many others will like the song.  I like slow ballad songs, but this one just doesn't appeal to me that much.  I'm sure if I have my heart broken by a girl I could hear this song for what it is, but right now it's not for me.  Its a great song and the story behind the lyrics is beautifully sad, but it's just not my personal pick.  I will say I like the use of horns though.  8.5/105. Satellite Call: The sound of this song is just pure sonic emotion.  The "woo oooh oooh"s of the chorus sound just tragically gorgeous. 9/106. Little Black Dress: At first I didn't like the song, because, I'm not a woman and I'm not gonna put on a little black dress.  But then I listened to it again and I could feel her emotion.  I listen to this song to hear her emotion and story.  The chorus is really catchy and heartfelt.  9/107. Cassiopeia: Another beautifully perfect song.  Her singing abilities are really showcased in the chorus.  I'm really starting to understand the hype for this album.  One of my favorite songs by anyone!  10/108. 1000 Times: This is one of the better of the three slower songs on the album in my opinion.  Great song to play while trying to get someone you love to swoon for you at the right moment.  The final chorus is sung in a trembling voice and you can really feel her words.  Beautiful.  9.5/109. I Choose You: This is a more upbeat and happy song.  The way she sings the chorus is candy to the ears.  Her voice really is sexy and gorgeous!  Think of the one you choose when you listen to this.  10/1010. Eden: The verses of this thumping song sounds soulful and funky.  Then the chorus turns into a delicious dance track.  The chorus really is pumping and catchy.  There are nice piano elements to the song as well.  Good pop.  9.5/1011. Islands: This is the best of the slow songs on the album.  This song reminds me of the recently discovered sister band HAIM.  This song brings out more emotion than the rest of the album with the background chants alone.  The chorus is just serenading perfection.  Feel the heartbreaking beauty of it for yourself.  10/1012: December: This song was just okay for me at first.  But the last part of the song really closes the album well and beautifully.  The layered vocals and guitar during the last 90 seconds make for a good ending to this surprisingly great album.  9.5/10So this album made me a believer.  I now believe this more than deserves its Album of The Year Nomination, and could possibly be the underdog and win.  It is a shame it hasn't been a megahit yet, but I'm sure more people are taking notice after hearing about the nomination.  Sara has one of the most beautiful voices working today, and I think she is much better and appealing than Adele honestly.  This is mature pop for everyone, especially those going through a break up.  The Blessed Unrest is definitely one of most unexpected pop masterpieces.  I'm a fan now and I more than recommend this album!

reviewText: After a five-year "hiatus" Barry White returns to the musical scene with a masterful release called "Staying Power."  Backed by the Love Unlimited Orchestra, as well as vocal support from Lisa  Stansfield, Chaka Khan, and ex-wife Glodean, White has put together another  winner filled with double-entendres, soothing melodies, and his own  patented style of "making love" in song.  The best cuts are the  title track, "Don't Play Games," "Sometimes," and two  versions of "The Longer We Make Love" (duets with Khan and  Stansfield, respectively).  Also, "the Maestro" remakes two hits  from the past: War's "Low Rider" and Sly Stone's "Thank  You."  The only downside is the use of a certain three-letter  expletive in the song "Get Up."  It is unfortunate that White who  appears to have a respect for women chose to insert the word which detracts  from an otherwise good selection.  That is the only thing that caused me,  as a listener, to reduce by one what could have been a five-star rating.

reviewText: Robert Johnson lived from 1911-1938, and died at the age of 27. But during his years active as a performing artist, 1934-1938, he recorded some of the best blues ever.The recordings had been lost for many years, but in 1961, Columbia released them on the vinyl release 'King Of The Delta Blues Singers.' The record inspired guitarists like Keith Richards, Eric Clapton and Robert Cray. It remains, even to this day, one of the most influential records of all-time.Overall, if you like the blues, classic rock or great guitar playing, than you need this album. Highly recommended for anybody who appreciates music.One of the best records ever released. Highly recommended! ENJOY!!!

reviewText: Seals and Crofts is perhaps one of the 70s strangest success stories.  It's hard to categorize their music...sometimes pop; sometimes folk; often rock; and even jazz.  But always dynamic, melodic and memorable.  Without possessing glamour-boy looks, they crafted elegant songs, often invoking personal religious beliefs, which in the future would stall their careers (the wonderful UNBORN CHILD).At any rate, the duo's entire catalogue finally made it to CD, including SUMMER BREEZE.The hit title song invokes the joys of both summer and a happily married man.  The album's other hit, HUMMINGBIRD, utilizes soaring harmonies and haunting imagery to assimmilate the gentle hum of the titular bird.The joy of S&C;'s music is you never knew what to expect---the playful feel of FUNNY LITTLE MAN; the raw energy of YELLOW DIRT and SAY; the exuberance of FIDDLE IN THE SKY; the sheer beauty of EAST OF GINGER TREES, ADVANCE GUARDS and THE BOY DOWN THE ROAD.Their use of instruments like the dulcimer and mandolin gave them an identifiable sound not heard by the pop/rock audiences.SUMMER BREEZE is an extremely entertaining album, expertly helmed by Louie Shelton and excellently remastered.

reviewText: Experimental Rock is so varied and even more experimental now than when this kind of Post-Shoegazing type of music started to slide to the mainstream and be accepted. This kind of melodic instrumentations are far too easy to copy and rip off and re-produce on the computer that most people can't tell the difference from one to another until someone sings on one of the songs.Sorry, but the Amazon reviwer gushes over EITS a little too much. I think EITS doesn't stretch far out enough, doesn't experiment far enough, doesn't try hard enough and sort of play the current-trendy theme tracks that get soon forgotten when the fad's gone. These tunes are far too light and easy, too catchy and obvious that yeah, sure they sound OK in the background but do you really remember the tunes afterwards? Not really - play M83 immediately afterwards or previously and I can guarantee you M83's tunes will remain in your head for much longer.Would EITS be as known or exposed as they are now if they hadn't done "Friday Night Lights"??? I doubt it.Yeah I can understand why you miss everyone all of a sudden - they left you because you're still doing the same thing you were doing 7 years ago, man. You need to move onto and really experiment, try something new, instead of playing this safe music. You've got the tools, so use them.

reviewText: I am always skeptical of reunion albums by old bands, even when they get good reviews, and initially this one was no exception. Then one day I heard "Blue Tip" on the radio when I was driving home for lunch, and it was so catchy that I ended up sitting in my driveway, waiting for the song to end before I could get out of the car. That hadn't happened to me in a long time. So I bought the album. Isn't that the way it's supposed to work? You hear a song on the radio and you like it, so you buy the album. I felt like a teenager again.And I'm happy to report that "Move Like This" has pretty much lived up to the praise it has been getting. I don't think it compares to the first four Cars albums, but I like it better than "Heartbeat City" and "Door to Door." I think it corrects the artistic wrong turn that the Cars took in the mid-eighties, when they morphed into an almost pure pop band.Sonically, "Move Like This" actually has more in common with the later stuff than it does with the first four albums. It does not have that mysterious late-night vibe that made the early albums so distinctive, and Elliot Easton's guitar is more restrained than ever. But what the new album does have that the previous two did not is a really nice groove. "Heartbeat City" had some good pop tunes on it, but it was a bit of a hodge-podge. "Door to Door" was similar in that way, but with fewer good tunes. By contrast, "Move Like This" has chugging rhythm guitars on all tracks except for the two ballads. It's very easy to listen to, and it's good driving music.The songwriting is solid throughout. "Blue Tip" and "Sad Song" are top-notch Cars songs. "Too Late" and the ballad "Soon" are not far behind. As usual with Cars albums, the second half is not as good as the first, but there are no clunkers. And it does sound like a Cars album, albeit a late period one. Greg Hawkes provides some of his distinctive blips and bleeps and whooshes on keyboards, while Elliot Easton adds just enough backbone with his guitar to keep things moving along. Although there are a few moments of déjà vu (e.g., the intro to "Sad Song," which sounds remarkably like the intro to "My Best Friend's Girl"), it doesn't sound too much like self-plagiarism either. Ric and the boys have updated the formula quite nicely. What an unexpected treat this album is.

reviewText: An album of undeniable historical importance, Free Jazz is also not likely to be one you'll listen to often. It inspired, and continues to inspire, countless great recordings of collective improvisations, including a number of far greater albums that followed immediately in its wake in the 1960s. Sun Ra's Magic City (and his other experiments in conduction), John Coltrane's Ascension (and Live in Seattle), Albert Ayler's New York Eye and Ear Control, and Peter Brotzmann's Machine Gun are all more spiritually searching, musically soaring and just plain searing experiences, and, while Ornette deserves all the props for doing it first, you can hear all the musicians on Free Jazz concentrating too hard as they try to make their solo statements or comment on what the other players are doing. It's all a bit tentative compared to what would come later, and, as a maelstrom, it's all rather polite. Interestingly, Eric Dolphy's bass clarinet comes off as the dominant and most confident voice. He's seems to have been born to channel some sort of ineffable cry from the soul, and it's no wonder that Coltrane wanted to be near him.

Aretha need not have worried about that, she was already in nationwide radio rotation.This (these) concerts are very enjoyable and are, at times, magnificent. They would have been better served to make it a single CD with those few non-repeated songs added on (there was certainly enough room on a single CD to do so).I like this concert very much, but it leaves me having to decide which disc to play as playing both becomes a bit tiresome with all its repetition.  However, the appearance of Ray Charles near the end of the first disc is certainly a highlight of the event.Overall, it is a strong Four Star release which would have earned another star if it had been put together better.

reviewText: I got this the day it came out but have waited til now to write a review as I wasn't sure about it at first and that is often a very good thing. As this is one of those albums that is a real grower, until one day all the pieces fall into place and you spend the next fortnight finding as much time as possible to listen to it.This is Will Sheff making a return to his youth back in the 1980's in hometown Meriden, NH. These are songs about growing up and a small world with the promise of so much more, best friends forever and summers remembered with rose tinted glasses. Jonathan Meiburg (Sheerwater) makes a much welcomed contribution with banjo, harmony and vocals and we have a harpsichord played by the uber talented Justin Sherburn. But the real talent is as always Will Sheff and his soaring vocals and imagery of lyrics that are closer to poetry than a `pop tune'.There are so many stand out tracks here `Lido Pier Suicide Car' is excellent and check out the versions on YouTube. `Stay Young' is an homage to the music of the eighties complete with fuzzy synth and if you try dancing to it, it only works if you do it eighties stylie, so large shoulder pads and rubbish bouffant may actually help. `Down the deep river' is almost anthemic, especially in length but it could go on all day as far as I am concerned, mind you then it would probably be `prog rock'.The opening number `It was my season' is one of those that yearns for the golden days and all that was promised and is just brilliant. There are so many instruments on this album and it all works including trumpet, lap steel and harmonica. The only track that seems out of place is `Walking without Frankie' which is a bit slow and brooding and brings the pace down a tad. The two final tracks are a joy especially album closer `Black Nemo' which is up there with any of Okkervil's best work. I am a bit biased as I have loved this band for four years but I still think this is a simply excellent life affirming good piece of music - even the cover art is great,; ok gush over I am off for another listen.

reviewText: Tesla was a bit different than the majority of the late '80s hard rock bands.  When one listens to "The Great Radio Controversy", one can detect Tesla's 1970's influences, whether it is Montrose, The Eagles,  Aerosmith, or Peter Frampton.  The result is a convincing exercise in hard  rock.This album contains "Love Song", perhaps the best known  song off this set.  "The Way It Is" has that Eagles influence all  over it, while "Heaven's Trial (No Way Out)" has an  Aerosmith-esque quality.  That's not to say the songs are derivative,  though; Jeff Keith's vocals are unique and give Tesla their own identity,  with a little help from guitar wizard Frank Hannon and sidekick Tommy  Skeoch.Of course, Tesla does whip out the heavy artillery quite often on  this album.  "Flight To Nowhere", "Hang Tough",  "Lady Luck", "Did It For The Money", "Party's  Over" and "Yesterdaze Gone" are excellent examples of the  band going for the throat, while "Be A Man" finds Hannon sliding  his way out of control in the intro before the song settles into an almost  country groove.  "Lazy Days Crazy Nights", "Makin'  Magic" and "Paradise" are examples of Tesla keen sense of  orchestration.  Piano timbres grace "Lazy Days" and  "Paradise", while the thick "Makin' Magic" uses guitar  orchestration to build drama.This is the most accessible out of Telsa's  cannon because it's got something for everyone: crushing hard rock  ("Flight To Nowhere"), tender ballads ("Love Song",  "Paradise") and acoustic blues ("Heaven's Trail") to  name just three genres.  Tesla will be remembered as one of the better  bands of the '80s hard rock explosion.

reviewText: "Invincible Summer," k.d.lang's 2000 release, was perhaps her most sultry, a collection featuring bossa nova beats and dreamy, looping electronics.  And then there's "The Consequences of Falling," the playful showstopper with which the singer opens the album.On this album, lang, who has a mezzo-soprano range, provided the vocals, of course.  What's more surprising is that she wrote, or had a hand in writing, most of the songs: all but "Consequences," in fact. Damian LeGassick, who backs her on guitar and keyboard, produced; the album carries work from virtually a full-sized pop orchestra.The song stylist has won both Juno Awards and Grammy Awards for her musical performances.  She has contributed songs to movie soundtracks and has teamed with musicians such as Roy Orbison, Tony Bennett, Elton John, Anne Murray and Jane Siberry.  This recording catches the Edmonton, Alberta, Canadian-born thrush in fine voice, at roughly the midpoint of what has now been her 25 year, multi-award winning career.  She first appeared on the scene in kitschy cowgirl outfits and spiky hair; in the clip I first saw of her, she's hopping continuously; I felt like yelling at the late-night television screen, "Sweetheart, you've got one of the greatest voices I've ever heard.  Leave the hopping to Herman's Hermits." But lang seems to have figured it out anyway, by herself.  Her early cover of Roy Orbison's "Crying," jump-started her career and remains one of her signature songs; "Constant Craving" is her biggest, Grammy-winning hit; "Miss Chatelaine" was also a sizable hit.The performer, who has come out as a lesbian, is also a vegan, animal rights, gay rights, and Tibetan human rights activist. She is a tantric practitioner of the old school of Tibetan Buddhism. She performed Leonard Cohen's "Hallelujah" live at the opening ceremony of the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, Canada: she had previously, performed at the closing ceremony of the 1988 Winter Olympics in Calgary.  The Times of London once said: "It's a quirk of the music industry that one of the sexiest, most sensual voices in all of pop music comes not from some raven-tressed siren in a glitter-dress but a middle-aged woman with a utility haircut and a penchant for male tailoring." And so it does.  Furthermore, she's a singer who can deliver finely phrased pop, a bit of jazz, a bit of country, a bit of a Latin touch.  And nobody can match her when it comes to belting out a hot torch song.lang frequently appears with the marvelous veteran jazz-pop crooner Tony Bennett, with whom she recorded the 2002A Wonderful Worldduets album.  Bennett just might be her number one fan; he once told the press "She's the best singer of her generation."  I am lucky enough to have seen this pair present the WONDERFUL WORLD repertory in person, at New York's Radio City Music Hall, in the most striking of circumstances.  Late September, 2001, about two weeks after the 9/11 destruction of the World Trade Center, and so much of downtown Manhattan. I had bought my ticket over the summer, and anxiously watched the papers to see if they would keep the date.  They did, and so did I. So did most of the ticket holders, I believe: there were empty seats, but not that many. Took ages to get through security, of course. You can believe that emotions ran high in that theater, on stage and in the audience: you could describe it as a love-in.  As it happens, I'd gotten the Radio City Music Hall ticket because I was just a bit nervous about seeing her in her more usual venues, with her more usual fans, in their hearty appreciation of her work.  Never mind, we all do just love that voice: it's wonderful winter, summer, spring, or fall.
summary: Wonderful Voice, Winter, Summer, Spring or Fall

reviewText: The King of Limbs is the Radiohead's eighth studio record, and comes on the heels of the impressive "In Rainbows". They are a band who possess one of the single most acclaimed discographies in rock, and even without the critics, they have fought hard to top themselves on each successive record.That's why this album is so underwhelming.TKoL is the sound of a band trying to step away from itself, and out of the shadow of it's own accomplishments. Everything about the record screams it, from the "Newspaper" special edition of the album (a package made of biodegradable material with the lifespan of a few years), the band's sudden and unceremonious release, or even it's short length.But the music itself says the most.Radiohead actually find themselves treading over old ground for once, striking a 50/50 mix between "Kid A" and Thom Yorke's solo album "The Eraser". The music is electronic and subdued, with the songs floating in and out without making much of a fuss. Nothing here rises above a middling tempo, and there are no big finishes to provide a moment of cathartic release like "Paranoid Android" or "Jigsaw Falling into Place". In fact, the whole album feels like it's always about to lift off, but never does.That doesn't mean it's a bad record by any means. It fits a mood - the rainy day, don't-want-to-get-off-the-couch kind of mood. The entire second half is actually very strong. "Lotus Flower" recalls "Idioteque" from Kid A, with a strong beat and a strangely soulful performance by Thom Yorke. "Codex" is one of the band's strongest piano ballads yet, with a murky, claustrophobic piano line contrasting nicely with some bright horn work. And "Separator" does indeed provide resolution, with what is probably one of Radiohead's most optimistic (and beautiful) sounding closers ever. In fact, if tracks two through four were left off, this would have been an incredible EP.But as it stands, I can't help the nagging feeling that they could've done better. This could have been released as an EP (which was entirely possible, as the Com Lag EP is actually one minute longer than TKoL), and thus avoided the criticism of a new "Radiohead Album". But instead, they have released what is possibly their "weakest" album, one that promises great things, but never fully accomplishes them.December 16th, 2011 EDIT:When I first wrote this review, Radiohead was maintaining a strong silence, giving little-to-no interviews on the album, and the band didn't fully reappear until a spate of TV appearances in September. In the light of some recent interviews they've given since, it's clear why it seemed to me like they didn't want to be Radiohead - because they don't. With The King of Limbs, they set out to step away from the pressure of releasing a ground breaking, classic "Radiohead" album each time around (a pressure that nearly broke them up during the recording of In Rainbows). In order to be true to themselves, they had to take a step away from themselves - they no longer want to make immense statements, but rather, enjoy themselves and what they do. In this, The King of Limbs is a huge success.

reviewText: 1998's Greatest Hits is the dream 2Pac album - possible the only one worth buying. All sides of 2Pac's music are displayed here - such tracks as 2 Of Amerikaz Most Wanted, California Love and Picture Me Rollin' are perfect for crusing in the Los Angeles sunshine in a black Mercedes - working with Snoop Dogg, Dr. Dre and Syke respectively. Life Goes On from 1995's All Eyez On Me album is sensitive poetry about ghetto life, ditto previously unreleased tracks Unconditional Love and Changes. Pac's trademark gangsta violence rap is unleashed in the rare Hit Em Up, performed with the Outlawz. It's a fitting tribute to one of gangsta rap's biggest ever figures. It is mind-blowing to think that 2Pac has sold more albums while dead than while alive; but maybe this double LP makes that statement a bit more understandable.

reviewText: Joy Division's `Unknown Pleasures' arrived in 1979 without warning or fanfare. Product inwards, this group was immediately different: austere, minimal graphics; monochrome, formal clothes; ascetic, modernist titles. And then there's the music, whose beauty, power, and long-term importance is hard to measure. In 1979, many things didn't exist in rock, and Joy Division, with this record, brought them into being. First, the idea that rock music could express emotions other than drugs, rebellion, youth, love: `Unknown Pleasures', for the first time in rock, expands the palette to include sadness, murderousness, self-hatred, despair; without apology, without embarrassment - like the entry of Greek Tragedy onto the rock stage. Without this, no Nirvana. No Husker Du. No Metallica, even. Second, an entirely new vocabulary. Melodic, dolorous bass, treated as a lead instrument. Baritone vocals, harsh, deep and dramatic, but with no interest in theatrics. Metronomic, disinterested percussion. Textural, ambient guitar that also bites, warps, and attacks. Third, production-as-aesthetic. The sound emerges out of inky blackness, prismatic like shards of broken glass: Noise and noise effects  are as important as structure. Many genres and many bands owe their existence and their careers to the simultaneous, unprecedented innovations this record makes. It is as groundbreaking and original - if not more - as Revolver, Axis: Bold as Love, Fun House, or Ziggy Stardust, in whose company it should be kept. In other words, a fundamental, utterly essential work for any rock music enthusiast.What about the songs? A brief glimpse into two key tracks (my favourites): `Shadowplay' follows some kind of imagined urban murder, charging through neon-lit darkness on the back of Albrecht's guitar: alternatively chordally violent, or flying through systemic solos that cycle like Reich or Glass. This will make your heart beat faster. `New Dawn Fades' starts up with bits of backward guitar-detritus, turning left into a requiem sung by a 20-year-old for his own life. It is utterly resigned and moving, and that would be enough; but towards its end it shifts up a gear and climaxes like no other song in rock; like despair finally expiated. Again, this one will have your hair standing up. Possibly the greatest single song in all of rock music, `New Dawn Fades' hits you with the Shock of the New. All these years later, it simply sounds thrown out of the void at us, fully-formed and totally unprecedented, and new with the original hurt every time. (Perhaps the nearest relative is `Tomorrow Never Knows'.)Unknown Pleasures is new-minted like nothing else in rock, utterly astonishing, and timeless. Off the scale in terms of creativity, emotional expression, dynamics, and the power to excite and rejuvenate, this record does everything a rock record has to do to be called classic, and then goes way further: into darkness; into creation.

Possibly the greatest single song in all of rock music, `New Dawn Fades' hits you with the Shock of the New. All these years later, it simply sounds thrown out of the void at us, fully-formed and totally unprecedented, and new with the original hurt every time. (Perhaps the nearest relative is `Tomorrow Never Knows'.)Unknown Pleasures is new-minted like nothing else in rock, utterly astonishing, and timeless. Off the scale in terms of creativity, emotional expression, dynamics, and the power to excite and rejuvenate, this record does everything a rock record has to do to be called classic, and then goes way further: into darkness; into creation.

reviewText: I enjoyed this album a lot, more than I initially expected. I read about the album before hearing the music and I wasn't sure I was going to like it, especially after seeing his videos for "Nancy" and "Hollywood", which I found a tad disturbing. Eventually I decided to give it a chance after seeing his performance on Letterman, which I absolutely loved. To my surprise, what I found was from start to finish I didn't really find anything I didn't like. For one, I like Josh Tillman's voice better than Robin Pecknold's. The songs here are a little more straightforward, musically, than any of the Fleet Foxes' stuff. I guess it would fit comfortably in the folk-rock genre, but there's bits of Americana, country and blues thrown in as well, with less of the vocal harmonies and elaborate instrumentation that dominate Fleet Foxes' music."This Is Sally Hatchet" is a standout for me, with the cathartic opening guitar chords and the really wonderful vocal melody, which is full of pleasant surprises. "O I Long To Feel Your Arms Around Me" has a Fleet Foxes vibe to it, with the organs and vocal harmonies in the background. It reminds me a little of the ending bit of Fleet Foxes' "Mykonos." "Tee Pees 1-12" has a definite country feel with the fiddles, and "I'm Writing A Novel" sounds like some unplugged version of a rock song you've heard somewhere but can't quite remember when.I think what makes this album interesting and special, though, is the lyrics. If you've been following Josh Tillman's Twitter account, you'll know that he has an extremely wonderful sense of humor and that he's pretty good with words. Some of the more interesting lyrics for me are in songs like "I'm Writing A Novel," "Hollywood Forever Cemetery Sings" and "Only Son of the Ladiesman."This man knows what he's doing.

Subsequent releases (particularly Thriller) would go on to cement his name in musical history (and IMO cause him to try and chase the record sales on future releases) I wish Mike would go back to this winning formula. Take one excellent producer (Quincy Jones) a backing group of top rate musicians (Paulino Da Costa, for example on Percussion) and live instruments, with great songs (by Michael himself, Stevie Wonder, Rod Templeton) This is one CD that you  can let play without skipping tracks. From the great 'don't Stop (`til you get enough) listen to the great percussion that under pines this track, to rock with you, Working day and Night, and the title track, just flow. One of the essential albums of the 70's, 80's.

reviewText: This album, like Tusk before it, suffers by comparison with the titanic success of Rumours, but what album doesn't? FM had moved on and were enjoying the luxury of being able to make art/pop with their own unique approach to arranging and the compelling character of the three independent songwriters.I would place this album as my third favourite FM album (of the Nicks/Buckingham era) although almost tied with Tusk which would be forth. I like the adventurous quality of the music. Despite the fact that they are attempting to echo a Rumours style sequence, they just can't help themselves and do a few interesting things along the way. Take the amazing vocal interplay between Lindsey and Christine McVie at the beginning of 'Eyes of the World' or listen to the sublime backing vocals on 'Can't go Back'. Stevie contributes the most substantial hit here with 'Gypsy' although for me over the years 'Straight Back' has become more and more superb. Give it another listen. It just blows you away. It would have to be in my top 10 FM songs of all time. Christine pens the catchy and nicely played 'Hold Me' which demonstrates that the band really know how to sell a song, no matter how slight and it's always nice to hear Christine and Lindsey dueting.Lindsey's songs are bizarre and wonderful, and also very catchy. I particularly like 'Empire State' but it could be an aquired taste. I prefer this album to the overproduced but still very decent 'Tango in the Night' album and you get the sense with both of these albums that the band is attempting to keep up with the times rather than serve up the straight up melodic blues of Rumours or the self-titled white album. It's innevitable that a band must keep moving and evolving while many of us would like them to stay put. Mirage is a smart, artistic and enjoyable pop experiment, very much of it's time.Love the album cover too, echoing the bizarre and compelling sexual dynamic of the band!

reviewText: A surprising Grammy this record is.  There's no way it could make much sales headway because the lyrics are almost uniformly bleak.  So bleak that about the only vocalist who could sing them other than Bob Dylan would have been Howlin' Wolf (and Dylan's become as raspy as the Wolf!).  Dylan pulls no punches and hits a dramatic peak right out of the gate on "Love Sick".  That track and "Not Dark Yet" are the most substantial additions to his vast repertoire, followed by the blues "Cold Irons Bound".The record closes with the 17-minute "Highlands", which begins poetically longing for a place of rest, then rolls off into a puzzling encounter with a waitress in a breakfast joint.  I'm guessing that this encounter is a sort of parable describing the unreasonable demands of an audience on an artist but the description is oblique enough that it could be an absurdist dead end.Daniel Lanois produces with more than his typical flair.  Much of the record seems to have been recorded using two bands and Lanois weaves their sounds in such a way as to provide a depth to the sound that must be heard to be appreciated.  The clever production is especially notable on the several blues numbers that Dylan sings.  As for Dylan's singing:  the voice ain't pretty but he's sings phrases with all the attention of a Billie Holiday.  She was also an arresting singer late in her career despite losing much of her vocal range.

Pop in this Do or Die classic and you can just see the Shining Rims Rollin on a Lexus, the City Lights and Chicago's Breathtaking Skyline. Get this Cd today if you don't own it yet.

reviewText: What is the difference between the death of neo-soul and the birth of freakquency? Erykah's statement on Worldwide Underground is about the world. She experiments with different sounds. Of course, this music is trippy, dark, soulful, and experimental. This is a EP that is way too long. It sounds like Badu just went into the studio and messed around with things. I only wish that she could've kept the original mix of "Love of My Life" on here. Instead she added the "worldwide" mix, without the original. The rest of the tracks except "Woo" and "The Grind" are great. What makes Worldwide Underground so special? Nothing, it's just a long EP full of experimental R&B. Come On Badu, when are you doing a full-length album? We have been waiting since 2001 for a new album. The drawings that Miss Badu created with a black ink pen are great. They look beautiful, but I wonder what they represent? Is it a sign that she is changing to different directions or is it just that she want us to visualize beauty? Overall, Worldwide Underground is one of those experimental hip-hop/R&B album that some listeners will love or just hate because it's different from her previously released records.
